hints.title: Translate both directions
hints.body: Treat necessity and sufficiency separately. The degree of the polynomial has not been fixed.
hints.recap: To refute an implication, an allowed example must satisfy its premise and fail its conclusion.
hints.pitfall: Do not silently restrict the polynomial to a cubic.
hints.pause: Look for simple polynomials on which you can count roots and stationary inputs exactly.

recall.reminder: To refute an implication, an allowed example must satisfy its premise and fail its conclusion.

hints.title: Try a factorable quartic
hints.body: A polynomial with a repeated factor can still have several distinct roots. Compare its roots with the roots of its derivative.
hints.recap: Differentiate the complete polynomial using the power rule, then factor the derivative.
hints.pitfall: A repeated root counts once, but may also be a stationary input.
hints.pause: Choose and analyse a simple quartic, checking every distinct input.

recall.reminder: Differentiate the complete polynomial using the power rule, then factor the derivative.

hints.title: Move the axis relative to a cubic
hints.body: Use a cubic with two stationary inputs, then vary its constant term and examine the resulting turning heights.
hints.recap: Turning heights determine how many times a continuous polynomial branch crosses the axis.
hints.pitfall: A constant vertical shift leaves all derivative values unchanged.
hints.pause: Construct a second example and use both to classify the two directions.

recall.reminder: Turning heights determine how many times a continuous polynomial branch crosses the axis.

solution:
P is not sufficient: f(x)=x4−x2 has exactly three distinct real zeros, but f′(x)=2x(2x2−1) also has three distinct real zeros.

P is not necessary: f(x)=x3−x+1 has derivative roots ±1/3, but both turning heights 1±2/(33) are positive. Its cubic graph therefore crosses the axis only once, on its left increasing branch.

Thus neither implication is valid in general. Answer D.
knowledgePattern: Separate exact root counts from lower bounds on stationary points
